newsitem.title: USA: Immune system recovery difficult for AIDS patients.
newsitem.headline: Immune system recovery difficult for AIDS patients.

text.p: The immune systems of AIDS patients lose diversity and therapies that fight the virus do not appear to restore the body's full array of disease-fighting cells, researchers said on Tuesday.
National Institutes of Health scientists report in the journal Nature Medicine that the new AIDS drugs do seem to boost the overall number of immune cells known as CD4+T cells.

But there are many different types of those cells, programmed to respond to specific disease threats. HIV infection reduces both the numbers and the diversity of the these cells. The drug therapies appear to increase the cell count, but not the diversity.

This adds to the growing evidence that HIV infected people should be treated early, before the virus does irreparable damage to the immune system. And it suggests that patients will need to keep taking preventive treatments to ward off the various diseases known as opportunistic infections that afflict AIDS patients.
Dr. Clifford Lane of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases said that even if certain types of T cells do not rebound, the body may be able to find ways of compensating.
Likening the cells to tiles in a Scrabble game, he said, "As the disease progresses, not only does an HIV-infected person have fewer tiles, but also fewer different tiles."

"If a person loses the letter 'z', they will be unable to spell out the word 'zebra.' However, if they have enough other tiles, they still may be able to describe a zebra by spelling a 'horse-like animal with black and white stripes,'" Lane said.

The team compared the immune systems of five sets of twins. In each set, one was HIV infected and one was not and were able to quantify the lack of diversity in the infected twin's set of immune cells.
They were also able to study the CD4 cells of a group of AIDS patients, tracking the decline of diversity as the disease progressed.

Neither the anti-retroviral drugs that have been proving successful in prolonging the lives of many AIDS patients, nor the experimental treatment with interleukin-2 have so far led to a recovery of the immune system's repertoire, despite some promising signs in earlier experiments.
